name: Jon Shirley
milestone_by_age_26: No material independent milestone by age 26 found. By his mid-20s he was a Radio Shack store/department manager (career start preceding Tandy's 1963 acquisition); major recognition came as Microsoft president/COO from 1983 (age ~45) through IPO leadership and 1990 retirement.
early_history_summary: Born in San Diego in 1938 to a Navy family, Shirley attended The Hill School and MIT, then spent roughly 25 years rising through Radio Shack/Tandy merchandising and computer division roles before Bill Gates recruited him to Microsoft in 1983.
family_context_summary: Born to Joseph and Mercedes Shirley in San Diego while his father was stationed in the U.S. Navy.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources as a technology or retail-domain advantage.
evidence_summary: Jon Shirley (b. 1938) built a long Radio Shack/Tandy career before becoming Microsoft president and COO in 1983 at about age 45, helping professionalize operations and guide the 1986 IPO. No dated, material breakout by age 26 is documented; early Radio Shack store management is ordinary early-career employment, not a verifiable age-26 success milestone under the rubric.

name: Niklaus Wirth
milestone_by_age_26: No material independent milestone by age 26. Born 1934; ETH BS 1958 (age ~24), MSc Laval 1960 (age 26), PhD Berkeley 1963 (age 29). First major language Euler 1965 (age 31); Pascal 1970 (age 36); Turing Award 1984.
early_history_summary: Swiss-born electronic engineering student at ETH Zürich who pursued graduate work in Canada and at UC Berkeley under Harry Huskey, then designed a sequence of influential languages (Euler, ALGOL W, Pascal, Modula, Oberon) as a Stanford and later ETH professor.
family_context_summary: Son of Walter Wirth (high school teacher / geography professor in some sources) and Hedwig (née Keller) in Winterthur, Switzerland.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was an educator (geography); not a computing-domain apprenticeship.
evidence_summary: Niklaus Wirth became one of computer science's defining language designers, but his career breakouts (Euler, Pascal, Turing Award) all fall after age 26. Completing a master's at age 26 is educational progress, not a material independent milestone under the rubric.

name: Vint Cerf
milestone_by_age_26: As a UCLA graduate student in Leonard Kleinrock's packet-networking group, contributed to ARPANET host-to-host protocol work and authored foundational early RFCs (including RFC 13, 18, and 20 on network control and ASCII interchange) in 1969 at age 25–26.
early_history_summary: Cerf grew up in Los Angeles, attended Van Nuys High with future ARPANET collaborators Steve Crocker and Jon Postel, briefly wrote analysis software for Rocketdyne Apollo engine tests while in high school, earned a Stanford B.S. in mathematics (1965), worked two years at IBM on QUIKTRAN, then entered UCLA for M.S./Ph.D. work that put him at the center of ARPANET protocol design.
family_context_summary: Born in New Haven to Muriel (née Gray) and Vinton Thruston Cerf; family later moved to Los Angeles. Father was academically high-achieving (Phi Beta Kappa); mother valued classical music and books.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were not computer scientists; advantage was educational aspiration and a bookish household rather than direct networking-domain transfer.
primary_early_advantage_tags: UCLA ARPANET, Kleinrock lab, Van Nuys peers Crocker/Postel, Stanford, Network Working Group, early RFCs, hearing impairment communications interest
evidence_summary: Vint Cerf (b. 1943) reached a material internet-pioneering milestone by 26: UCLA ARPANET host-to-host work and early RFCs in 1969, collaborating with high-school peers Crocker and Postel inside the Network Working Group. He later co-designed TCP/IP with Bob Kahn (1973–74), led DARPA networking programs, and became a Turing Award and Presidential Medal of Freedom recipient and Google's Chief Internet Evangelist. Early leverage combined elite institutions, scarce packet-networking facilities, and an exceptional peer cohort rather than inherited industry capital.
starting_point: Born 1943 in New Haven to Muriel and Vinton Thruston Cerf; raised in Los Angeles with a hearing impairment in a bookish, academically ambitious household.
current_position: Living internet pioneer; long-time Google Chief Internet Evangelist (from 2005; role reported through mid-2020s) and widely recognized co-designer of TCP/IP.

trajectory.event: Earned B.S. in mathematics from Stanford and began systems engineering work at IBM on QUIKTRAN.
As a UCLA graduate student in Kleinrock's group, contributed to ARPANET host-to-host protocols and authored early RFCs including RFC 20 (ASCII network interchange).
Completed Ph.D. at UCLA and joined Stanford as assistant professor working on packet network interconnection.
With Yogen Dalal and Carl Sunshine specified the first TCP (RFC 675), building on open-architecture internetting ideas developed with Bob Kahn.
Joined DARPA and funded development of TCP/IP, packet radio, packet satellite, and network security programs.
Shared the ACM Turing Award with Robert Kahn for pioneering internetworking and TCP/IP.
Received the Presidential Medal of Freedom and joined Google as vice president and Chief Internet Evangelist.

early_history_summary: Hyderabad-born systems/networking researcher who trained at IIT Madras and CMU (Seshan), did SDN-related postdoc work at Stanford with Nick McKeown, then built a faculty career at Wisconsin and UT Austin with impact on data-center networking and cloud systems.
evidence_summary: Aditya Akella is a well-cited networking systems professor (UT Austin Regents Chair; ACM Fellow), but Wikipedia and CVs reviewed do not list a birth year. Without age verification, IIT/CMU degrees and later awards cannot be certified as age-26 milestones.

name: Gavin Kliger
milestone_by_age_26: In early 2025 at age ~25, appointed as a high-profile Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) engineer with operational authority across multiple federal agencies after rising to senior software engineer at Databricks with reported seven-figure compensation.
early_history_summary: UC Berkeley EECS graduate (2020) who spent roughly five years as a software engineer at Databricks, then left a high-paying industry role in January 2025 to join DOGE, later becoming U.S. Department of Defense chief data officer in March 2026.
primary_early_advantage_tags: UC Berkeley EECS, Databricks senior engineering, DOGE appointment, Bay Area tech ecosystem
evidence_summary: Multiple 2025 press accounts describe Kliger as about 25 when he joined DOGE after a Berkeley EECS degree (2020) and senior engineering tenure at Databricks (including claims of leaving a seven-figure salary). That public operational appointment—and subsequent 2026 DoD chief data officer role—constitutes a material, dated milestone by age 26. Birth year is inferred as ~2000 from consistent '25-year-old' reporting in early–mid 2025; family background is not documented.
starting_point: Not documented in reviewed sources beyond U.S. origin and UC Berkeley EECS education culminating in a 2020 degree.
current_position: Chief Data Officer at the U.S. Department of Defense (appointed March 2026); former DOGE engineer and Databricks senior software engineer.

trajectory.event: Graduated from UC Berkeley with a B.S. in electrical engineering and computer science.
Joined Databricks as a software engineer and rose to senior engineer over about five years.
Joined DOGE in the second Trump administration, exercising operational roles across USAID, CFPB, IRS, USDA, USAGM, and FTC.
Appointed Chief Data Officer at the U.S. Department of Defense after DoD DOGE work including GenAI.mil.

evidence_summary: Richard V. Andree (1919–1987) is a thin-biography figure whose published computing/math milestones (1958 algebra text; ALPS on Bendix G-15; Pi Mu Epsilon awards named for him) post-date age 26. No independently verified achievement by 1945 was found.
